title: Davenant’s close: defects in regenerate works are not appropriately second-sense mortal
source_text: XXXIII. Quibus observatis probat defectus culpabiles, qui bonis renatorum operibus adhaerent, licet vere peccata sint, & secundum strictum legis rigorem mortem mereantur, & propterea quandoque a scriptoribus nostris mortalia nuncupentur, interea tamen non debere singulariter & appropriate, secundo, scilicet, sensu jam explicato, mortalia peccata vocari. Quod inter alia hoc argumento demonstrat; Illud peccatum appropriate mortale appellatur, quod inducit novum reatum mortiferum, donec eluatur novo actu poenitentiae. Sed peccatum quod adhaeret bonis operibus renatorum, utcunque juxta rigorem legis, posset damnare hominem extra Christum, tamen renatum & in Christo insitum non modo non damnat; sed neque novo aliquo reatu involvit. Nam cum quilibet renatorum habeat in se quasi duos homines, novum & veterem Adamum, quicquid vetus Adamus tumultuetur, & reluctetur legi, non imputatur homini renato & novo normam legis pro posse suo sequenti, & rebellionem concupiscentiae aversanti, & quantum in se est refrenanti.
pass_a_gloss: Which things observed, he proves that culpable defects which cling to the good works of the regenerate, although they are truly sins and according to the strict rigor of the law merit death, and are therefore sometimes called mortal by our writers, yet ought not in the meantime to be called mortal sins singularly and appropriately—namely in the second sense already explained. Which among other things he demonstrates by this argument: That sin is appropriately called mortal which induces a new death-bringing guilt until it is washed away by a new act of repentance. But the sin which clings to the good works of the regenerate, however according to the rigor of the law it could damn a man outside Christ, yet does not only not damn one regenerate and grafted into Christ; but neither involves him in any new guilt. For since any of the regenerate has in himself as it were two men, the new and the old Adam, whatever the old Adam may tumultuate and struggle against the law is not imputed to the regenerate and new man who follows the norm of the law as he can, and turns away from the rebellion of concupiscence, and restrains it as much as in him lies.
pass_b_english: Davenant’s hinge: work-adhering defects are true sins by law, yet not appropriately ‘mortal’ in the second sense.
They add no new death-guilt while the new man resists the old Adam’s tumult—unlike capital falls needing fresh repentance.

choices.why: Technical restriction of the mortal label.
